# Overview

The most comprehensive and definitive set of metrics on the importance of the fisheries for Pacific Countries is the Benefish reports, with @Benefish4's _FISHERIES in the ECONOMIES of Pacific Island Countries and Territories_ being the latest publication in a series of four. Significant effort went into compiling and publishing the report. Weighing in at 705 pages, Benefish4 is indeed a meaty tomb.

The process involved two consultants[^authors] visiting the fisheries and statistical agencies of 24 Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs) to collect and ground-truth the myriad of different metrics they sought to collect. In-country time was limited to a couple of days within each PICT, together with lead up and post-visit engagement with the specialists from each area; however, the _scale_ of the report included: 

* A fisheries-oriented discussion of macroeconomics, 

* Country information on specific topics (fisheries production, contribution to gross domestic product [GDP], etc.), 

* A discussion of important topics across all countries (e.g. the regional significance of access and exports of fishery products), 

* Comparisons with results of previous Benefish studies, some important features of the benefits from fisheries that have emerged from this study, and 

* Recommendations on improving the measurement of fisheries benefits and assuring the continuity of those benefits. 


This project focused on extracting as much data as possible from Benefish4 pdf publication and making it available electronically. During the process, inconsistancies have been addressed as much as practical.

\newpage

# Recommendations for Future Reports.

1. The Benefish publications, as a single report, is too broad to do justice to all the topics inside it. Quite simply the report contains too much stuff. Its breadth comes at the cost of being _comprehensive_ on its covered topics; for example, the treatment of aquaculture.  

Future reports should consider the scope of what's being collected, and focus more attention on collecting data from each. The report itself, in "Chapter 36 Recommendations", reaches a similar conclusion.

2. Alternative data collection processes need to be developed to both shorten the compiliation time, and improve data quality, again echoing Chapter 36.2 of the report.

Every report involves a large amount of lead-up time and in-country data collection. Four year data collection processes introduce the high risk that every new Benefish report is like a new box of chocolates to the member country supply data into SPC: you just never know what will be found. Repeated data collections are needed to build up both a feel inside of SPC and memeber countries for what the true metrics are, and "muscle memory" associated with regular statistical reporting according to a common set of metrics. 

3. More use of administrative data sources need considered. For example, FAME data on data sheet log collections, and Vessel Monitoring Systems should be able to reconcile with PICT systems. If they do, then reporting from FAME data sources might replace in-country data collection processes.

Before the project could head down this path, significant effort needs to be invested in data collection systems and processes, including into the statistical classifications and standards infrastructure that could support a robust data collection process. 

4. FAME needs to revisit the costs and benefits of the severity of its data governance constraints. For FAME data's use as an administrative data source for fisheries statistical reporting, SPC would need to revisit its "General Policies: Governance of fisheries, aquaculture and marine ecosystem data provided to SPC by its members" policy.[^datapolicy] 

The policy provides a framework for how SPC handles any fisheries, aquaculture and marine ecosystems related data including the data handling, ownership, security, sharing, integration and dissemination. However, it is too restrictive and prevents FAME data being used to produce high-quality economic, and fisheries-related statistics for the Pacific.

a. Using administrative data sources for statistics is no longer seen as a "misuse" of administrative data.

Statistics New Zealand faced similar trade-offs in its Integrated Data Infrastructure(IDI)[^IDI] between maintaining the public's trust around the analytical use of confidential information, versus using administrative data for generating more accurate aggregate statistcs that reduce respondent burden. It recently released a proposal to use IDI information as an "administrative data-first" approach to the New Zealand Census.[^Admin] 

The "case for change" focused on the reduced cost, greater resilience, and more efficient reuse of existing government data to make outputs more flexible and frequent.[^caseforchange] The same benefits apply for FAME data sources. Statistics New Zealand's consultative approach might serve as a model for revisiting the rigidity of SPCs existing data policies.

5. The report needs to be modenised and its output be capable of electronic manipulation. Significant effort has gone into _this_ project just to extract numeric information from a pdf-based report. PDF reports as "output" from a research project have no place within the 21st century.

Some of these metrics are best replaced with measures from FAME's administrative data sources; for example, "Catches by Method" might be derived from FAME's Catch and Effort statistics and our coastal data.

Similarly, SDD might have better, more timely and more comprehensive measures of Fish Exports than currently collected through the Benefish publications.

Other aspects of the report to explore are whether the topics in Table \@ref(tab:ThermaticTopics) are the correct topics for data collection around. Fishing contributions to GDP, with two different approaches might be metrics collected through SDD efforts related to expanding National Accounting collections within the Pacific. 

Metrics missing from the current Benefish publications, but maybe which should be included, are fishing activity measures; for example, the vessel numbers and change like Figure \@ref(fig:PurseSeineBoats) below from our FAME data

# Aquaculture
Gillett, in chapter 35.5, highlighted the scarcity of information about national aquaculture production as a significant finding from the study. One of the most outstanding points about aquaculture in the region – and perhaps one of the most
remarkable observations during the study – was the lack of knowledge of the overall aquaculture production in almost every PICT. Indeed, he felt: "Considering the enormous amount of development funds and public money spent on promotion of
aquaculture in the region, it is amazing that there is so little monitoring of the progress of aquaculture development in terms of the total volume and value of production."

## Incompatible Volume and Value Data
That same lack of confidence in the data is also apparent when the value of aquaculture reconciled against its volume components: tonnes and pieces. The volume and value metrics bear no systematic relationship to each other because, if they did, then techniques like regression analysis or simultaneous equations analysis would estimate a non-negative separate implicit aquaculture prices per tonne and per peice. Attempts to allocate the value to the volumes through estimating an implicit price failed to produce non-negative values, implying that neither the volume nor the value aquaculture measures related to the each other.

## Domestic Fish Consumption

Domestic fish consumption is a metric with changing collection metrics across countries, significantly complicating cross-country comparisons. Most of the source information for this component resides in the qualitative elements of the Benefish text. For example, the Kiribati domestic fish consumption metrics are encapsulated as twelve bullet points of reference to other studies spanning a range of time periods between 1989 - 2016, with new infromation included from the 2019/20 Household Income and Expenditure Survey. 

Very little of the fish consumption metrics are quantitative, and where they are (for example below), they are subject to significant cross-country measurement variability.



## Fisheries Revenue


```{r FR, echo=FALSE}
   
      ##
      ##    Estimate US$ for non-US$ currencies
      ##
         Fisheries_Revenue <- merge(Fisheries_Revenue,
                                   Exchange_Rates,
                                   by.x = c("Unit", "Year"),
                                   by.y = c("Currency", "Year"),
                                   all.x = TRUE)
                              
         Fisheries_Revenue$ToUSDollar <- ifelse(Fisheries_Revenue$Unit == "US$", 1, 
                                          ifelse(Fisheries_Revenue$Unit %in% c("Pieces", "Tonnes"), NA, Fisheries_Revenue$ToUSDollar))
                                   
         Fisheries_Revenue$USDollarEquivalent <- Fisheries_Revenue$Value / Fisheries_Revenue$ToUSDollar
         Fisheries_Revenue <- data.table(Fisheries_Revenue)
         
         Aggregate_Values <- Benefish_studies[,
                                         list(USDollarEquivalent = sum(USDollarEquivalent, na.rm = TRUE)),
                                         keyby = list(Member_Country ,
                                                      Year,
                                                      Harvest_Sector)]

        
```

# Next Steps
At the start of this project, the plan was to upload the cleaned Benefish data int SPC's .Stat system. However, after discussions with SDD, the cleaned data might be better suited being uploaded into SPC's Data Hub as the CSV files they're currently existing as. The move from .Stat to the Data Hub recognises the variables within the tables are still quite idiosyncratic for each country source, despite being grouped thermatically.

Secondly, more planning around the structure and the content of the next Benefish report is needed, to be able to identify which elements might be replaced with administrative data, which components can come from other sources, like SDD, and which components need a dedicated data collection system developed that supports the on-going collection of data.
